title: Time Lab™

instructionalStandard.rule: Discovery precedes formal explanation when the concept is meant to be revealed through investigation.

competencies.label: Observe actual time and attention allocation
competencies.definition: Uses a record or trace to compare intended time use with what actually happened.

competencies.label: Distinguish observation from interpretation
competencies.definition: Separates what was recorded from the story, judgement or explanation attached to it.

competencies.label: Prioritise what matters
competencies.definition: Uses importance, urgency, cost and personal purpose to identify what should receive protected time.

competencies.label: Form a testable explanation of a time pattern
competencies.definition: Builds a bounded working explanation involving context, attention, friction or environmental pulls and states what would challenge it.

competencies.label: Design a workable time experiment
competencies.definition: Defines one small rule or response, a realistic boundary, a prediction, a restart plan and a failure signal.

competencies.label: Apply and record the method in real life
competencies.definition: Attempts the chosen response in suitable real-world opportunities and records outcomes without treating a missed opportunity as failure.

competencies.label: Review evidence and adapt
competencies.definition: Compares prediction, action and outcome; identifies uncertainty; and makes a justified adjustment.

competencies.label: Transfer the method
competencies.definition: Applies the inquiry method to a new time or attention situation and explains what transfers and what changes.

days.title: Where did the time go?
days.purpose: Create a discrepancy between the learner's time story and observable traces before teaching a time-management model.
teaching: Time is finite, but the first teaching task is noticing rather than optimisation.
A behavioural pattern is something that happens; it is not a character label.

beats.label: Story: the person with no time

learnerEvidence.description: One bounded record of where time or attention went, plus what the learner expected.

days.facilitatorFocus: Do not diagnose the learner. Make the discrepancy visible and leave the explanation open.

days.title: Thinking like an investigator
days.purpose: Teach evidence discipline so the learner can investigate time without confusing judgement with observation.
teaching: Memory, intention and records are different evidence sources.
Observation describes what happened; interpretation proposes why.
Useful evidence is specific enough to test or revisit.

beats.label: Discover: two descriptions of the same event

learnerEvidence.description: Distinguishes observation from interpretation in a worked example.
Names one real time situation to investigate.

days.facilitatorFocus: Correct evidence language, not personality. 'I am lazy' is not an observation.

days.title: Build the investigation
days.purpose: Bridge learning into the 90-minute Time Lab Phase A, where the learner maps the pattern, forms an explanation and designs the experiment.
teaching: A useful investigation needs a specific situation, a working explanation, a prediction and a test.
Prediction creates something that later evidence can disagree with.
days.labPhaseAOutcome: Time Lab Investigations 1–6 produce the time map, cost, personal equation/falsification test, contract, prediction, restart plan and failure signal. Formal post-discovery explanation remains for Day 4.

learnerEvidence.description: A testable prediction linked to the chosen pattern.
A bounded time experiment with rule, protection, restart and failure signal.

days.facilitatorFocus: Keep the 45-minute bridge separate from the 90-minute Lab. Do not pre-empt the Lab revelation.

days.title: What the investigation revealed
days.purpose: Give formal language to patterns the learner has already encountered in the Lab.
teaching: Time use is often shaped by attention, cues, friction and environmental pulls.
A time leak is a repeated allocation with a meaningful cost, not any leisure or rest.
Priority and protection are design choices, not moral scores.

beats.label: Apply concepts to my own map

learnerEvidence.description: Explains one personal pattern using evidence and distinguishes what is observed from what is inferred.
Applies the formal model to the learner's existing time map.

days.facilitatorFocus: Explanation should feel like recognition: name what the learner has already seen.

days.title: Evidence, not guilt
days.purpose: Teach honest experiment recording and perform the first evidence checkpoint.
teaching: An opportunity, an attempt, an outcome and a missed/no-opportunity day are different records.
Evidence quality matters more than looking successful.
One observation can update a method without proving a stable change.

learnerEvidence.description: Correctly distinguishes opportunity, attempt, outcome and no-opportunity.
First bounded review of experiment evidence; method adjustment only if evidence supports it.

days.facilitatorFocus: Do not turn adherence into virtue. Protect honest records, including failure and no opportunity.

days.title: When the plan meets real life
days.purpose: Use weekend/field evidence to diagnose barriers and make one justified adjustment.
teaching: Barriers are information about the design and context.
Restarting is part of self-management.
Environment can reduce the amount of willpower required.

beats.label: Revise one part of the method

learnerEvidence.description: One evidence-linked change to the rule, environment, first step or restart plan.

days.facilitatorFocus: A revision must point to evidence. Avoid changing the goal simply to improve the percentage.

days.title: Protecting what matters
days.purpose: Widen from one time leak to prioritisation, focus protection and age-appropriate leverage without abandoning the experiment.
teaching: Urgent and important are not the same.
Protection can include scheduling, boundaries, batching, elimination or delegation where appropriate.
Leverage changes how effort is allocated but does not remove accountability.

beats.label: Apply to a real upcoming demand

learnerEvidence.description: Uses priority/protection reasoning on a new real demand.
Final experiment opportunity/outcome is recorded outside the teaching example.

days.facilitatorFocus: Do not present busyness as achievement or rest as waste. The test is alignment with what matters.

days.title: What does the evidence support?
days.purpose: Close the seven-day test and teach bounded interpretation of the learner's evidence.
teaching: Rates require honest denominators and clearly defined opportunities.
Prediction and outcome can differ without either being a moral failure.
Evidence supports a bounded conclusion; it does not define the person or prove lasting change.

learnerEvidence.description: Experiment counts/rate with provenance to recorded opportunities.
Evidence-backed conclusion, uncertainty and next adjustment.

days.facilitatorFocus: Ask 'what does this evidence support?' before 'did you improve?'

days.title: The meta-time skill
days.purpose: Make the method portable beyond the original time pattern.
teaching: The deeper skill is noticing, investigating, testing and adjusting.
Near transfer keeps much of the context the same; farther transfer changes the situation.
Transfer is demonstrated by a new application, not by saying 'I can use this anywhere'.

beats.label: Apply the method to the new situation

learnerEvidence.description: Applies the method to a new time/attention context and explains what changed.

days.facilitatorFocus: Do not count a transfer intention as transfer evidence; require a concrete new application.

days.title: Show what you can now do
days.purpose: Demonstrate the method, compare starting and later evidence, build a useful portfolio narrative and identify the next pathway.
teaching: Progress is described through the strongest available evidence, not a single score.
Self-report, task performance, real-world evidence and transfer answer different questions.
The learner's next step follows from the evidence gap, not from a personality label.

learnerEvidence.description: Demonstrates the inquiry method on a new scenario using an authored rubric.
Source-linked synthesis of starting point, application, evidence review, adaptation and transfer without repeating private raw responses.

days.facilitatorFocus: The close should tell the learner what the evidence shows, what remains open and what to practise next.

reportingBoundary: This blueprint creates evidence opportunities. It does not convert completion, self-report or one experiment into a durable competency claim. Competency progression is classified only from qualifying source-linked evidence.
